title: Unpinned autobrew fetch left unverified third-party static libraries inside four installed shared objects
claim: curl, fs, V8 and xml2 each fetched https://autobrew.github.io/scripts/<name> during configure and dot-sourced it into the running shell; the prebuilt static libraries that script downloaded are now linked into curl.so, fs.so, V8.so (47,520,328 bytes) and xml2.so. Proven three ways: the install log's 'Using autobrew bundle' lines (fs :721 libuv-1.52.0, curl :784 curl-macos-8.14.1, V8 :1258 v8-14.6.202.26, xml2 :1556 .deps fingerprint), otool -L showing no corresponding dylib, and strings finding libcurl/8.14.1, 14.6.202.26, 2.14.4 and libuv tokens inside the .so files. magick did NOT fetch - Homebrew was detected so its macOS branch was skipped and its other branch is Linux-x86_64 guarded; magick.so links Homebrew ImageMagick dynamically. The selector script is unpinned and unchecksummed on a mutable GitHub Pages path and is refetched on every build; the bottle URLs inside it are version-labelled. Each package's cleanup then deleted the script and the extracted archive (fs uses rm -f, which cannot remove the .deps directory).
impact: Install-time arbitrary code execution as the building user, and - the part that outlives the install - roughly 49 MB of unverified third-party binary resident in the library, dyn.loaded into every R session that calls library(nflreadr). WS-B's 90/90 tarball PASS does not cover these binaries: they were fetched BY those tarballs at install time, entirely outside CRAN's chain of custody. Grepping install logs for 'autobrew' is a false negative - xml2's script contains zero echo statements and never appears in the logs. What the bundles contained on 2026-07-26 is unrecoverable.
recommendation: Rebuild the library from binaries (Posit Package Manager, type='binary') so configure never runs and the artefact is one CRAN-checksummed object. If source builds are required, set DISABLE_AUTOBREW=1 (USE_BUNDLED_LIBUV=1 for fs) on an egress-restricted host and verify with otool -L that each .so links a real dylib. Record otool -L for curl.so, fs.so, V8.so and xml2.so as a build-provenance artefact. Track CVEs against libcurl 8.14.1, libxml2 2.14.4, libuv 1.52.0 and V8 14.6.202.26 - statically linked copies receive no OS patching.

title: No integrity verification anywhere before deserialization; live network bytes stream straight into readRDS
claim: A grep for checksum|sha256|sha-256|md5sum|digest::|signature|gpg|verify.*hash|hash.*verify|integrity across all six targets' entire R/ source returns zero matches, as does a grep for any TLS override (ssl_verifypeer, ssl_verifyhost, insecure, CURLOPT_SSL*). nflreadr/R/from_url.R:65-78 opens a bare url() connection and hands it directly to readRDS - bypassing the curl R package's handle API (not libcurl, which url() still uses internally), so there is no intermediate buffer where a check could be inserted. The pattern is independently re-implemented at least three times (nflreadr::rds_from_url, nfl4th:::raw_rds_from_url, nflfastR:::load_raw_game/read_raw_rds) and none of the three added a check the others lack. Every cached artefact is plain gzip with no integrity field beyond gzip's non-cryptographic CRC32.
impact: The entire trust chain reduces to TLS to the resolved host plus GitHub's access controls over who can publish a release asset to nflverse/nflverse-data, nflverse/nfldata, nflverse/nfl4th or nflverse/nflplotR. A payload that decodes to a structurally valid but factually wrong data frame - spoofed scores, altered lines, tampered win probabilities - is accepted with no warning and flows into anything downstream. That outcome needs no code-execution vulnerability at all. nfl4th's model path adds a second, C++-side deserializer (xgboost::xgb.load.raw) after the first.
recommendation: Do not let nflverse fetch inside a production request path. Mirror each release asset into Dime-controlled storage, record a SHA-256 at ingest, and verify that pinned hash on every read. Treat any hash change on a historical asset as an event to review before promotion. nfl4th's own cached_model() is.raw() format-sniff is not a safety check - a malicious raw vector passes it trivially.

title: Offline fetch failure is silent, is cached as a success, and keeps being served after connectivity returns
claim: In the offline+cold run all six calls returned normally: not one raised an R-level error. load_schedules(2026) returned a 0x1 frame after three warnings (connection failure, nflreadr's own cli_warn, and a twice-fired Unknown or uninitialised column: 'roof' from its own post-processing), because rds_from_url downgrades the try-error to cli_warn and returns data.table::data.table(). memoise sees that as an ordinary cacheable value; the cache directory went from 0 files to 5. A three-step reproduction confirmed the poisoning: same cache dir, same URL, called again fully online, returned dim 0x1 in 0.013s without retrying the network. Independent review reproduced this end to end and found it worse than reported - zero conditions are raised on the poisoned re-read. Cache keys are hash(url) only, with a fixed 24h TTL baked into nflreadr's .onLoad and no connectivity-aware or content-aware invalidation; the only escapes are nflreadr::clear_cache() or waiting out the TTL.
impact: A cron job or model run that loses connectivity for a single call silently proceeds on zero rows, and keeps doing so for up to 24 hours after the network is healthy, with no exception to catch and - on the re-read - not even a warning. Warnings are the only signal and are trivially lost to suppressWarnings(), options(warn=-1), knitr or any log router. Filesystem cache mode makes this a multi-hour trap; the default memory mode confines it to one process, which is why a fresh Rscript per job masks it.
recommendation: Wrap every loader call in an explicit non-empty assertion (nrow above an expected floor) and fail hard, because the package will not. If filesystem caching is used, call nflreadr::clear_cache() after any run that emitted a fetch warning. Better: cache in Dime's own layer keyed on an explicit successful-fetch flag rather than relying on memoise, which cannot distinguish a legitimate empty result from a cached failure.

title: Live game state for a decision-support computation is fetched over cleartext HTTP
claim: nfl4th::get_4th_plays() builds a plaintext http://site.api.espn.com URL by paste0() at sources/nfl4th/R/get_game_data.R:41-42 and fetches live in-game state from it. It is the only cleartext endpoint among all endpoints actually fetched by the six targets - every other fetched endpoint is https. (The static census contains other http:// strings that no package's code ever fetches, e.g. nflfastR's doc-only citation of www.nflgsis.com.) The payload is JSON via jsonlite::fromJSON, so the R-deserialization risks in NFLV-002 do not transfer to it. No pattern in the scan matched this - it was found by reading the file.
impact: Live game state feeding a real-time 4th-down and win-probability computation crosses the network without TLS, so it is readable and modifiable by anyone on the path. For a real-money product this is decision-support input with no transport integrity whatsoever.
recommendation: Do not use get_4th_plays() on any wagering surface as shipped. Either source live game state from a TLS endpoint Dime controls, or proxy the call through an https gateway and validate the response shape before it reaches the model.

title: V8 executes bundled JavaScript inside the R process with the JS-to-R escape hatch enabled by default
claim: V8::v8()'s R-level default is console = TRUE (R/V8.R:136), and bindings.cpp:541-548 installs the console object whenever that flag is set. R/callback.R then exposes four R primitives to JavaScript: console.r.call (eval(parse(text=...)) then do.call), console.r.get (eval(parse(text=...))), console.r.eval (source(textConnection(...)), arbitrary R in the global environment) and console.r.assign (assign(..., globalenv())). Three bundled JS assets execute in the R process via V8: juicyjuice/inst/dist/bundle.js (css_inline.R:19-22), reactR/inst/www/babel/babel.min.js (babel.R:20-25) and reactable/inst/htmlwidgets/reactable.server.js (reactable.R:850). All three ctx$source() calls in the closure were verified to read system.file() paths, not URLs - though V8's own documentation demonstrates URL sourcing twice, once over plaintext http.
impact: The JavaScript-to-R boundary is not a sandbox by default. No path in this closure currently feeds untrusted JS to a context, so the exposure is latent rather than live - but the guard rail is off, roughly 30 MB of bundled JS was not reviewed, and these three bundles' blast radius is in-process rather than browser-sandboxed.
recommendation: If Dime code ever creates a V8 context, use V8::v8(console = FALSE), which skips console_template() entirely, and never pass an http(s) URL to ctx$source(). V8 enters this closure only through nflplotR -> gt -> juicyjuice and reactable; if gt table rendering is not needed, dropping nflplotR removes V8, its 47.5 MB unverified binary and this JS surface together.

title: nflfastR add_dakota() load()s a remote .Rdata into a live function frame
claim: sources/nflfastR/R/aggregate_game_stats.R:687-691 opens url('https://github.com/nflverse/nflfastR-data/blob/master/models/dakota_model.Rdata?raw=true') and calls load(con) inside try(silent=TRUE). load() is a strictly larger trust surface than readRDS: rather than returning a value the caller inspects, it deserializes an entire saved workspace's named objects directly into the calling frame. The code then trusts that a variable named dakota_model appears - pre-initialised to NULL so a failed or tampered load degrades to 'model unavailable' - and passes it straight into mgcv::predict.gam(). WS-C promoted this above every other deserialization row in the closure for exactly this reason. The host is a 4th distinct nflverse-org data repo (nflfastR-data), confirmed present once in the closure URL census.
impact: Reached from calculate_player_stats(weekly=TRUE). A tampered .Rdata could define any object in a live function frame, not just the expected model, and the silent-degradation design means a substituted or missing model produces no error - the same fail-quiet pattern as NFLV-003, here applied to a model rather than to data.
recommendation: Avoid the dakota code path, or vendor dakota_model.Rdata into Dime-controlled storage with a pinned hash and load it yourself before calling nflfastR. This finding was source-verified, not live-tested - calculate_player_stats(weekly=TRUE) was not one of the exercised loaders.

title: nfl4th performs an unconditional DNS lookup and can delete a user cache file on every library() call
claim: sources/nfl4th/R/zzz.R .onLoad calls curl::nslookup('github.com', error = FALSE) unconditionally - confirmed live by tracing curl::nslookup during library(nfl4th) in a fresh Rscript --vanilla process, not only by source reading. The same hook creates tools::R_user_dir('nfl4th','cache') if absent, and otherwise calls file.remove() on the games cache file when that file exists and options(nfl4th.keep_games) is not TRUE. On this host the delete branch was a no-op: the directory pre-existed the audit (mtime Jul 26 21:26) and held no games file. There is no option that skips the lookup itself - nfl4th.keep_games only changes what happens after it.
impact: library(nfl4th) - including transitively via library(nflverse), which attaches all five core packages - is a network operation and a potential filesystem mutation before any nfl4th function is called. In a locked-down deployment that is unexpected egress; in a long-lived container it silently discards cached game data on each load. No other target package sets environment variables or writes to a cache at load time.
recommendation: Set options(nfl4th.keep_games = TRUE) before loading if the games cache matters, and redirect all three packages' caches with R_USER_CACHE_DIR (it governs nflreadr via rappdirs and nfl4th/nflplotR via tools::R_user_dir). Include github.com DNS resolution in any egress allowlist, or do not load nfl4th in processes that must not touch the network.

title: future's .onAttach sources .future.R from the current working directory into the global environment
claim: sources/future/R/zzz.R:97-167 - .onAttach calls sourceFutureStartupScript(), which with R_FUTURE_STARTUP_SCRIPT unset and no future.startup.script option resolves to c('.future.R','~/.future.R'), checks the current working directory FIRST, and source()s the first match with local = FALSE, i.e. into the global environment. It is opt-out, not opt-in; errors are downgraded to a warning. The trigger is an explicit library(future) or library(furrr) attach, NOT library(nflverse) - WS-C's original reachability claim was too broad and was corrected by Imports-vs-Depends analysis and empirically disproven with a marker test. No .future.R exists anywhere it would be found on this host and no override is configured, so it did not run here.
impact: Any R process that attaches future or furrr with an untrusted working directory executes that directory's .future.R at global scope, where it can define or overwrite anything the session later uses. Relevant to CI runners and to any job that changes into a checkout it does not fully control. Not reachable from the nflverse load path itself.
recommendation: Set R_FUTURE_STARTUP_SCRIPT=FALSE (or options(future.startup.script = FALSE)) in the environment of any process that attaches future or furrr, and never attach them with an untrusted cwd.

title: Remote image bytes reach the system ImageMagick parser through nflplotR
claim: magick's install-time autobrew branch demonstrably did NOT fire: Homebrew was detected ('Homebrew 6.0.12' in the install log) so configure:51-52 was skipped, and configure:31 is guarded on uname -sm being Linux x86_64 so it is dead code on darwin/arm64. magick was installed twice; the first attempt failed on a missing Magick++.h from imagemagick@6 and the successful run linked Homebrew ImageMagick 7 dynamically. What remains is E10: image_read(<url>) feeds remote image bytes into the system ImageMagick parser, reachable from nflplotR's logo and headshot rendering, and magick/src/base.cpp:12 sets KMP_DUPLICATE_LIB_OK=1 at package init.
impact: Untrusted remote image bytes reach a large C++ image-parsing surface that this audit did not read. Classified accepted-risk rather than finding because the fetch is author-initiated, not automatic, and because - unlike the four autobrew statics - this ImageMagick does receive OS-level patching.
recommendation: Keep Homebrew ImageMagick current. Do not render images from URLs Dime does not control. nflplotR's own bundled logos are 39 raw PNG blobs inside sysdata.rda (all verified to carry a valid PNG magic header) and need no network fetch.

title: CC-BY-4.0 attribution conditions apply and nflverse expressly disclaims that its grant covers the underlying NFL data
claim: nflverse/nflverse-data is CC-BY-4.0 - confirmed via api.github.com and by reading the full 18,647-character LICENSE.md. GitHub's structured summary lists permissions commercial-use, modifications, distribution and private-use, with conditions include-copyright and document-changes. Section 3(a) sets out the attribution requirements (creator identification, copyright notice, license notice, warranty disclaimer, URI, indication of modifications) and Section 4 extends them to sui generis database rights over a substantial portion of the contents. A search for non-commercial language across all 90 DESCRIPTION and LICENSE files, the full license text, and every fetched nflverse document returned 0 hits. However nflreadr's own Terms of Use state 'The R code for this package is released as open source under the MIT License. NFL data accessed by this package belong to their respective owners, and are governed by their terms of use.', and CC-BY-4.0 Section 2(b)(2) states 'Patent and trademark rights are not licensed under this Public License.' No affiliation or trademark disclaimer of any kind was found anywhere in nflverse's own documentation.
impact: Attribution is conditioned on Sharing the licensed material, which a public-facing product surface may or may not constitute. Separately, nflverse declines to assert that its grant reaches the underlying NFL-originated facts, and the grant expressly excludes trademark - so NFL team names, logos and 'Next Gen Stats' are unaddressed by it. NFL.com, Next Gen Stats, Pro Football Reference and FTN Fantasy terms of service were outside the audit's approved network scope and were not reviewed. This audit reaches no legal conclusion.
recommendation: Take the 9-item list in ws-e/commercial-posture.md section 5 to counsel before any nflverse-derived data reaches a user-facing surface. Priority order: whether Dime's use constitutes Sharing under 3(a); whether nflverse holds the rights it is licensing; separate NFL trademark clearance; upstream vendor terms, particularly FTN Fantasy as a named commercial vendor. Implement a concrete attribution notice once counsel sets its scope - this audit found no evidence Dime displays one today, and did not check.

title: 14 GPL-family and 4 weak-copyleft packages sit in the hard-dependency closure, two of them first-order
claim: Of 90 packages: 72 no copyleft, 4 weak (LGPL/MPL), 14 GPL-family - re-derived independently from license-inventory.csv. All 6 targets are MIT + file LICENSE. data.table (MPL-2.0) is a DIRECT Imports of 5 of the 6 targets (nfl4th, nflfastR, nflplotR, nflreadr, nflseedR), verified edge by edge in dep-edges.csv; gsubfn (GPL >= 2) is a direct Imports of nflseedR and pulls proto (GPL-2). No AGPL exists anywhere in the closure - the 2 apparent grep hits are MPL-2.0 Section 1.12 'Secondary License' boilerplate in data.table/LICENSE and vctrs/LICENSE.note. Two file-level grants hide inside otherwise-permissive packages: stringi ships stri_stats_latex() under GPL-2.0-or-later inside a BSD-3-Clause-style package, and vctrs ships src/order-*.c and src/order-*.h under MPL-2.0 inside an MIT package. highr, knitr and mime declare a bare 'License: GPL' with no version qualifier at all.
impact: GPL/LGPL/MPL obligations are conventionally understood to attach on distribution rather than internal use, and the absence of AGPL - whose trigger is network use - is what makes a server-side-only reading available at all. Whether Dime distributes (a customer-facing artifact, a Docker image handed to an external party, a published fork) is an architectural fact this audit did not investigate. None of the copyleft exposure originates in nflverse's own code.
recommendation: Confirm with counsel which distribution scenario applies. If any image or artifact containing these packages leaves Dime's control, work data.table's MPL-2.0 file-level share-alike first (first-order on 5 of 6 targets), then gsubfn/proto on nflseedR, then the bare-GPL trio. Note that the whole GPL rendering toolchain (rmarkdown, knitr, highr, mime, base64enc, bitops, htmltools) enters only via nflplotR -> gt.

title: Two upstream nflverse data feeds have already died
claim: nflverse's own automation-status article (last_built 2026-04-20T17:32Z per pkgdown.yml) states for injuries: 'Our data source died after the 2024 season. At the moment, there is no 2025 data and there is no ETA yet as to when we will be able to make injury data available again.' For participation: 'Participation data prior to 2023 is from NFL NGS. The data source died during the 2023 season. Participation data from 2023 onwards is courtesy of FTN and is provided after all post-season games are completed. It does not update during the season!' Other feeds carry documented cadences: schedules every 5 minutes in season, rosters daily 07:00 UTC, PFR snap counts 4x daily, depth charts daily with a post-2024 source change.
impact: dictionary_injuries (16 fields, documented back to 2009) has no current data and no replacement source. Participation lost in-season freshness entirely. This is nflverse's own admission, and it makes upstream feed death demonstrated history for this pipeline rather than a hypothetical risk. Distribution is a single point of failure: GitHub Releases on one org's repos, updated by GitHub Actions.
recommendation: Do not build a product surface that depends on nflverse injury data. Treat participation as post-season-only. Monitor the automation-status article as a tracked operational dependency, and define a per-feed fallback before adoption - mirroring (see NFLV-002) also protects against a feed disappearing mid-season.

title: Dime's nfl_games schema discards the betting lines and results nflverse already ships
claim: dictionary_schedules (45 fields) ships away_score, home_score, result (home minus away), total, overtime, away_moneyline, home_moneyline, spread_line, away_spread_odds, home_spread_odds, total_line, over_odds, under_odds and div_game. Dime's nfl_games table (drizzle/nfl.schema.ts) has none of these - no score columns, no line columns, nothing betting-related; it is purely a schedule and metadata table. nflverse also carries an espn column alongside its composite game_id, structurally the same key as Dime's event_id primary key, so the join is available.
impact: The single highest-relevance gap for a betting product. Historical closing lines and results are exactly what backtesting and model calibration require, they are already present in the frame Dime is closest to ingesting, and Dime currently drops them. Backfilling lines later is materially harder than capturing them at ingest.
recommendation: Extend nfl_games, or add a sibling nfl_game_lines table, with the score, result, total and line/odds columns before ingesting schedules, so lines are captured from the first load. Join on the espn column rather than reconstructing nflverse's composite game_id.

title: memoise's filesystem cache readRDS makes the closure's unverified-deserialization trust persistent
claim: memoise's filesystem backend is four lines (cache_filesystem.R:36-51): cache_has_key tests file.exists, cache_get calls readRDS and returns the result as the memoised function's value with no type, structure or provenance check of any kind. cache_s3.R:52 and cache_gcs.R:55 are the same shape against a downloaded temp file. nflreadr wires this in at .onLoad around rds_from_url, csv_from_url, raw_from_url and parquet_from_url; nflplotR and ggpath do the same. Cache entries are always written as RDS regardless of the source format, keyed by rlang::hash() over the function source hash plus the URL - never by content and never by any server ETag or Last-Modified.
impact: Converts the transient, per-session trust decision in NFLV-002 into durable on-disk state that is re-deserialized on every subsequent session. Anyone with write access to the cache directory controls what the loaders return, indefinitely. Did not run on this host - no filesystem cache directory existed by default.
recommendation: Treat the nflreadr cache directory as a trust boundary: a dedicated path with restrictive permissions, never shared between users or jobs. Prefer the default memory mode plus Dime-side persistence over filesystem mode, which is also the mode that makes NFLV-003 a multi-hour trap.

title: knitr's R_KNITR_OPTIONS is an environment-variable code-injection point
claim: knitr exposes R_KNITR_OPTIONS as an environment-variable-to-eval path (defaults.R:218-235) - a genuine Low finding distinct from, and not isolated by, the general rendering surface. Everything else escalated under E8 sits downstream of an explicit knit() or render() call on a specific file and is gated on options$eval; nothing fires at load, and knitr's .onLoad does package-local initialisation only. No rendering has occurred on this host. rmarkdown's implicit source('./global.R') / source(server.R) / load(.RData) paths are Shiny-only and shiny is not installed.
impact: Any process that can set R_KNITR_OPTIONS in the environment of an R process that later renders a document gets an eval. knitr is present as a hard dependency via nflplotR -> gt -> htmlwidgets even if Dime never renders anything, so the package is loadable regardless of intent.
recommendation: Do not let untrusted input reach the environment of R processes. If Dime never renders R Markdown, note that knitr, rmarkdown, tinytex, markdown and litedown are in the closure only because nflplotR hard-Imports gt - dropping nflplotR drops the whole rendering toolchain.

title: The nflverse v1.0.3 git tag points at a commit whose DESCRIPTION declares 1.0.2
claim: git ls-remote resolved the tag format as v<version> (not guessed). nflverse's v1.0.3 tag points at commit b8314c594a93 (2022-10-05) whose DESCRIPTION still declares 1.0.2; the real release commit is the next one, 6c4f6ad, 'release v1.0.3 to cran (#19)', 2023-08-14 - the tag was created roughly 10 months early and never moved. Both comparisons were run and emitted in full: against 6c4f6ad, 19 differing files (18 CRLF-only plus DESCRIPTION); against the literal tag, 20 differing files (17 CRLF-only plus DESCRIPTION, NEWS.md's 4-line 1.0.3 entry, and README.md's 40 lines). Every file under R/ and NAMESPACE is CRLF-only against either base - no R code changed. The other five targets' tags all match their DESCRIPTIONs and CRAN exactly.
impact: A maintainer bookkeeping defect, not tampering - it has no effect on shipped code. It does mean the v1.0.3 tag cannot be used naively as a provenance anchor for nflverse 1.0.3: anyone verifying against it sees a version mismatch that could be misread as divergence. More generally, git tags are mutable and this one demonstrates they can be misplaced, so tag-based verification is corroboration rather than proof.
recommendation: If Dime pins nflverse by git ref anywhere, pin commit 6c4f6ad rather than the v1.0.3 tag, and record why. Prefer the CRAN tarball plus its published MD5 as the provenance anchor for all six targets.

title: nfl4th hides its CRAN-detection string as raw bytes so a source grep will not find it
claim: nfl4th/R/cache.R:127 calls grepl(rawToChar(no_cache), ...) where no_cache is a raw[6] vector stored in sysdata.rda. Decoded with Rscript --vanilla it is the string 'ripley'. The package detects that it is running on a CRAN check machine by grepping the cache path for that name, and stores the needle as raw bytes so CRAN's own source grep will not match it. No pattern in the scan matched this; it was found by loading and decoding the binary payload. The same inspection of all four targets' sysdata.rda files found no function objects, no closures carrying environments and no executable content anywhere.
impact: Benign in effect - it only changes caching behaviour on CRAN check machines. It is deliberate evasion of a policy inspection in form, and it demonstrates concretely that a source-level grep of these packages is not a complete control.
recommendation: Weigh it as a maintainer-trust signal for nfl4th specifically. Any re-audit should decode sysdata.rda and other binary payloads rather than relying on source greps alone - treat 'no pattern matched' as 'no pattern matched', never as 'nothing there'.

title: A Dime memory note describes a kickoff_time_et column that does not exist in the implemented schema
claim: The project memory note kickoff-datetime-convention.md states the schema shape is kickoff_utc (instant), kickoff_date (DATE), kickoff_time_et (display). The implemented schema - drizzle/nfl.schema.ts nflGames, confirmed byte-for-byte against drizzle/0118_dark_gateway.sql - has no kickoff_time_et column. Only kickoff_utc (timestamp), kickoff_date (date) and time_valid (boolean) are persisted; ET display time is derived at read time from kickoff_utc, not materialized.
impact: Documented-intent versus implementation drift on Dime's own side. Anyone writing an ingestion mapping from nflverse's gametime field - which IS stored, always in Eastern time regardless of venue, per dictionary_schedules - against the memory note will target a column that does not exist. nflverse persists precisely what the note says Dime should.
recommendation: Correct the memory note to match the implemented schema, or add the column deliberately. This is a cheap alignment either way, and it should be settled before any nflverse schedule ingestion is written against it.

title: Dime and nflverse disagree on team abbreviations for at least 2 of 32 teams
claim: Dime stores ESPN-sourced abbreviations directly in nfl_teams.abbreviation (confirmed in scripts/data/nfl-2026/teams.json): Rams = LAR, Commanders = WSH. nflreadr's team_abbr_mapping - the 143-entry alias-to-canonical table shipped as package data - canonicalizes to Rams = LA and Commanders = WAS. The other teams checked agree: Raiders LV, Patriots NE, Packers GB, Saints NO, Buccaneers TB, 49ers SF, Chargers LAC.
impact: Any join between Dime's nfl_teams.abbreviation and an nflverse frame keyed on team abbreviation silently drops or mis-attributes Rams and Commanders rows - silently, because both sides are valid non-null strings and no constraint catches it. Two teams is 6% of the league and includes a division rival pair.
recommendation: Do not join on abbreviations. Join on ESPN numeric ids, as the project's own fbs-team-crosswalk convention already mandates for CFB, and apply nflreadr::clean_team_abbrs / team_abbr_mapping as an explicit canonicalization step wherever an nflverse abbreviation must be used.

title: Seven closure packages carry call-time execution surfaces that were accepted rather than closed
claim: Reviewed and accepted, none of which ran on this host: tinytex (downloads and runs a TeX Live installer, osascript sudo prompt, automatic brew install ghostscript); parallelly (launches processes including over SSH); Rcpp (compiles and dyn.loads C++, plus a load() of a cache index whose default location is the session-private tempdir(), not a persistent user directory); xfun (shell-outs and uploads, all explicit developer functions unreachable from rendering, plus a persistent R_user_dir cache readRDS); rmarkdown (implicit source('./global.R'), source(server.R), load(.RData) - Shiny-only, shiny not installed); data.table (update_dev_pkg() over an HTTPS project repo by explicit call; base patching hard-gated on R < 4.0.0); litedown (an exec engine that runs chunk-named commands, plus a cache readRDS). Eleven further escalated packages were reviewed and found benign outright, including stringi, whose icudt download is proven not to have occurred - the file ships in the tarball and is md5-verified against a manifest inside it.
impact: Each requires an explicit call that the nflverse data path does not make, so none is live today. Together they enlarge the surface materially if Dime's own code ever calls into the rendering or parallel toolchain, and several of them are present only as transitive tooling nobody chose deliberately.
recommendation: Keep them out of production images if rendering and parallelism are not needed. Re-evaluate this row specifically if Dime adds document rendering, PDF export or parallel simulation - nflseedR's simulator pulls future/furrr, so the parallel path is one feature away.

title: Release-asset downloads terminate on a host that appears nowhere in the static URL census
claim: GitHub release-asset URLs return HTTP/2 302 to https://release-assets.githubusercontent.com/... (a signed, time-limited URL), verified two independent ways: curl -sD - -L from the shell and curl::curl_fetch_memory() called from R, both against a real loader URL (.../releases/download/players/players.rds). That hostname appears nowhere in the 90-package static census (0 hits, case-insensitive) - expected, since it is minted per request and is never a literal string in any source file. It is also not the objects.githubusercontent.com name the audit plan anticipated. The raw/master/... path used by load_schedules redirects instead to raw.githubusercontent.com, which IS in the census (404 occurrences).
impact: Not suspicious. It matters operationally: an egress allowlist derived from a static source census would block every release-asset download while appearing complete, and R-level fetch hooks cannot observe it because redirect-following happens inside libcurl below any R-level hook.
recommendation: Any egress allowlist must include release-assets.githubusercontent.com and raw.githubusercontent.com alongside github.com, and must be validated against observed traffic rather than derived from source greps.

title: 932,557 lines of C/C++ and roughly 30 MB of bundled JavaScript were not read
claim: 932,557 lines of C/C++ across 2,497 files in top-level src/ trees; counting any path containing /src/ gives 933,771, the extra 1,214 lines being test fixtures not part of any installed shared object. 38 of 90 packages ship src/ and all 38 declare useDynLib (native-code-inventory.md records cachem as an exception, but cachem/NAMESPACE:17 is useDynLib(cachem, .registration = TRUE)); all six targets ship zero native code (verified, not assumed). Four packages are roughly 77% of the mass (715,263 of 932,557 lines): stringi 540,791 (bundled ICU 74), xgboost 83,413, vctrs 49,363, sass 41,696 (bundled libsass). A targeted native pattern scan found 97 hits total: 68 getenv (documented config vars), 14 system (11 of which are the words 'system (' inside ICU comments, 3 a git clone in a libsass dev script), 8 dlopen (all in vendored upstream trees), 6 setenv, 1 popen, and ZERO exec*() and ZERO fork() anywhere in the closure. Roughly 30 MB of inst/ web assets were also unreviewed; three of those bundles execute in the R process via V8 (see NFLV-005). Both ws-c/escalations.md L1 and ws-c/escalation-reviews/STRUCTURAL-LIMITATIONS.md L1 still quote ~892,000 lines; native-code-inventory.md documents that figure as wrong and supersedes it with 932,557.
impact: The exposure is volume plus transitive supply chain: ICU, libsass, cmark-gfm, libyaml, yajl, cctz, utf8lite and xgboost's dmlc/rabit have their own maintainers, release processes and CVE histories, none in scope. Compensating evidence is real and worth stating - these bytes are byte-identical to what CRAN publishes, verified across three sources, so 'tampered in transit or locally' is removed as a hypothesis even though 'safe' is not established.
recommendation: Highest-value next step is a CVE map of the named vendored versions (ICU 74, libxml2 2.14.4, libcurl 8.14.1, libuv 1.52.0, V8 14.6.202.26, libsass, cmark-gfm) - roughly half a day, and it produces an actionable patch list. Version-diffing the vendored copies against upstream releases converts about 700k of the lines from 'unread' to 'unmodified relative to a named release' for 1-2 days of work.

title: nflreadr's three most important behaviour-controlling options are absent from the installed documentation
claim: nflreadr.cache, nflreadr.verbose and nflreadr.cache_warning never appear in any Rd topic's usage or argument section of the installed help (checked via tools::Rd_db); only nflreadr.prefer and nflreadr.download_path do. The three exist solely as internal getOption() reads inside non-exported functions in R/zzz.R and R/from_url.R. None of the six packages writes its own options into the options table at load time - every one reads with a default= fallback at call time - so options() introspection after library() reveals nothing about them. The installed binary namespace was confirmed byte-identical to the staged source for these functions.
impact: The knobs that govern caching - the mechanism behind NFLV-003 and NFLV-014 - are discoverable neither from the installed documentation nor from runtime introspection; you have to already know the names. nflreadr.cache in particular is read exactly once at .onLoad, so setting it after library(nflreadr) has no effect on the already-memoised functions.
recommendation: Set these explicitly and early in every Dime R runner - options(nflreadr.cache=...) BEFORE library(nflreadr) - and record the intended values in Dime's own runbook rather than relying on upstream documentation that does not mention them.

title: The shipped nflverse dictionaries contradict each other and themselves on field types
claim: dictionary_pbp documents game_id as type=character with the description 'Ten digit identifier for NFL game.', but the live format is the underscore-joined season_week_away_home string produced by nflverse_game_id(). dictionary_schedules carries the correct prose for the same field but declares type=numeric, which cannot be right for a string containing letters and underscores. espn_id is declared numeric in dictionary_rosters and character in dictionary_players and dictionary_depth_charts. height/weight are character in dictionary_rosters and numeric in dictionary_players. nflfastR's teams_colors_logos Rd claims '36 rows and 10 variables' while its own format block lists 15 fields. Two frames have loaders but ship no dictionary at all: load_teams() and load_rosters_weekly().
impact: Type declarations in the shipped dictionaries cannot be used to generate an ingestion schema without verifying against actually loaded data. An automated mapping that trusts them gets game_id, espn_id and height/weight wrong.
recommendation: Derive Dime's ingestion types from a loaded sample rather than from dictionary_* type columns. Treat espn_id as a string everywhere, which Dime's own ESPN-id join convention already does. Do not expect dictionary coverage for load_teams() or load_rosters_weekly().

title: The two CRAN mirrors named in the audit plan turned out to be a single origin
claim: cran.wu.ac.at does not serve its own copy - it answers with HTTP/2 301 to cran.r-project.org - and cloud.r-project.org is a CloudFront CDN (via ...cloudfront.net, x-amz-cf-pop LAX54-P1) in front of the same CRAN master. Their byte-identical indices are therefore not independent corroboration and were not reported as such. Independence rests entirely on the designated fallback ftp.osuosl.org (effective host ftp2.osuosl.org), a genuine rsync mirror on separate infrastructure, from which all 90 tarballs were re-downloaded (90/90 HTTP 200) with sha256 matching primary 90/90. Across the parsed indices (24,409 mainline records on primary and mirror2, 24,408 on osuosl) the primary-versus-osuosl comparison found 8 version differences and 1 primary-only package - all ordinary mirror lag, osuosl behind in every case and never ahead - and same-version-but-different-MD5 = 0.
impact: Bounds what the 90/90 PASS actually proves. Agreement with CRAN's published MD5 proves the local tarball matches what CRAN serves today; CRAN publishes no signatures for source tarballs, so there is no cryptographic chain back to the maintainer. The osuosl cross-check narrows the gap - an attacker would need both CRAN master and an independent mirror - but does not close it.
recommendation: When re-verifying in future, choose the second source by infrastructure rather than by hostname: check for 301 redirects and CDN response headers before treating two mirrors as independent, and record which host actually served the bytes.
